utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Could the registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-99-36-PT, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I shall first ask Mr. Brdjanin and General Talic whether you can hear me in a language that you can understand. Mr. Brdjanin, please. THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General Talic? THE ACCUSED TALIC: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances. The Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner and Andrew Cayley for the Prosecution, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Appearance for Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm John Ackerman. I appear with my co-counsel, Milka Maglov, from Banja Luka, and we have an interpreter with us by the name of Ms. Ratislava Mirkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And for General Talic?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am Natasha Fauveau, attorney at the Paris bar. I represent Mr. de Roux and Mr. Pitron, who are counsel for Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if I may -- I know that Your Honour has your own agenda, but I wonder if I may ask that Your Honour goes into closed session straight away because there is matter which we need to raise which is of some urgency in the light of an order that we've had from Your Honour giving us a deadline of 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Permission granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please to go in closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, closed or private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The request is for a closed session, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Cayley tells me it could be private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I understood that you wanted a closed one. So it will be a private one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I will deal first with the aspect of motions, pending and decided. You know that last Friday, the Appeals Chamber delivered its judgement on the motion by General Talic for leave to appeal against the decision of Judge Hunt of the 23rd of November, 2001. I would imagine that you have been served with a copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci. So that brings me to something which is of relative importance because more or less it's become a formality more than anything else. But as far as the fourth amended indictment, now we have a final decision. And I think I would proceed by asking the Defence counsel for both the defendants whether it is their desire that I have the fourth indictment as amended and as updated by the Prosecution following the decision without -- Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm very sorry. But by our records it may be that there is actually still one final outstanding motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is one motion by General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Of a request for dismissal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. But that's going to be decided.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour doesn't feel that that will have any effect on the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, actually, it's with regard to all the proceedings -- all the pre-trial proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the request. It doesn't refer specifically to the indictment or to the substance of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I think -- Your Honour, that's probably right. I don't think it does. It is more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically, I mean, the decision may ultimately, if it's in favour of General Talic's motion, will obviously bring us back to square one, and our efforts would have to more or less be redirected elsewhere and start possibly again. But it does not affect what I'm saying now, in actual fact now. The matter of the indictment as such and the objections and preliminary pleas that were raised with regard to the fourth amended indictment have now been settled, and I think we could proceed with the reading, unless there is an exemption forthcoming from the Defence side. And I would ask Mr. Ackerman first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would waive any reading of the indictment. However, I think the indictment that we're actually operating on right now is called something like corrected fourth amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the other thing, I think - although I could be told by the registrar in just a second that I'm wrong about it - but that indictment has not been translated into B/C/S and served upon the defendants. That would be a problem, if that's the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that would be a problem, if that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think that's the case, but I'm not positive about that. And I wouldn't have raised it now unless you raised it. And I wish I'd checked before I walked in here before I started talking about it, but I think that's the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There's something wrong with -- Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with the concern that Mr. Ackerman expressed as regards the translation of the indictment into Serbo-Croatian; however, I should also add that I -- and here I'm sure, because I checked. I know that the pre-trial brief of the Prosecutor was not translated into Serbo-Croat either. Therefore, in these proceedings before the Tribunal, the brief gives additional clarifications, and it's considered as an annex to the indictment. If the brief has the additional details about the charges in the indictment, and if the accused does not have the brief, then there's no logic here. I think not only the indictment must be translated into Serbo-Croat but also the pre-trial brief has to be translated into Serbo-Croat. I'm sure, Mr. President, that you will agree with the concern that I'm expressing because of the right of the accused to have -- to be familiar with the charges in his own language is one of the fundamental rights of Defence, and the Statute of this Tribunal has enshrined that concept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner. I think the first of these points has to definitely be clarified, whether the fourth -- the corrected fourth amended indictment has been made available also in the language that the defendants understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm happy to say, Your Honour, it's absolutely nothing to do with us. It's the Registry who deals with those matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It has to be established.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We'll have to find out from the Registry whether that's happened. We don't know. We haven't been told one way or the other, and we wouldn't be told. It's not a matter for us. Can I say in respect of the pre-trial brief, I don't know whether it's been translated or not. But it's fair to say we had a response, as Your Honour knows, so that instructions must have been taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will understand, Ms. Korner, that's why I said the first of these is more important to me, because the other one was -- as you said, in respect of whether it was translated or not, followed up by response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think the -- we will be making a find-out to see whether the corrected fourth amended indictment has been translated and whether it has been amended. I think your other objection that the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution may not have been translated into B/C/S or made available to your clients in B/C/S is not that important, for the very simple reason that following that pre-trial brief, you entered a response -- a formal response, and that would nullify any legal objection that -- Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to join that objection. And I'm looking right now -- it's my recollection - and of course my recollection is not always correct - that upon the service of the pre-trial brief and receipt of an order to respond to it within a fairly short period of time, I filed a motion asking for an extension of that time. And part of the basis, I believe, of my motion was that it had not been translated into my client's language and, therefore, I was unable to consult with him about it. And it's my further recollection that that motion was denied and I was ordered to file it on the date that had been suggested. So I think I have raised the issue some time ago. And it's my further understanding that it was only last week that the Registry undertook any effort to have it translated. And I'm getting ready to look -- and if I'm incorrect about that, I will certainly let you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And we will be checking, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So there is an outstanding motion, to which I referred last Friday during the Pre-Trial Conference that we had. And as promised, that will be decided before we start our labours on Wednesday. There is also another outstanding motion filed by Mr. Ackerman relating to your objection to Rule 92 bis procedure, and this, I think, was handed down or is being handed down today. The decision has been -- yes. Okay. Because actually, what happened was it was ready on Friday. I had it signed, but then between one thing and another, it remained on my desk, and I doubt whether it reached the Registry in time -- in time on Friday and, therefore, one had to change the date after that. But in any case, I think if you haven't had it, you should be having it this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we're talking about the same motion, I think we got it on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then it may have reached -- I may have -- yes, because actually, I left my Chambers and I walked in, and it suddenly dawned on me that I left it at my desk. So -- but you had it on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we haven't had it. I'm not sure -- it was a ruling on Mr. Ackerman's objection to the Rule 92.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, about the Presiding Officers not being present --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Two different ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- walking out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's the one I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We have it, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then, of course, as you say, there is another objection, another motion or objection by Mr. Ackerman with respect to Rule 92 bis admission of witness statements number one. Okay. That was filed on Friday. But there is one -- there are the four motions by Mr. Ackerman to delay the testimony of four witnesses to which reference was made amply during Friday's sitting. There were actually five. As you recall, one was decided orally with respect to Mr. Donia. The other four I reserved to decide upon orally either today or on Wednesday. Actually, the idea was today because we had meant to start the trial on Monday. However, now probably they will be decided on Wednesday unless in the meantime, as a result of the exchange of documents that should have taken place if it has taken place, one or more of these motions are going to be withdrawn. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we supplied Mr. Ackerman with all the documents that were mentioned in the motion, but over the weekend, I understand from Ms. Gustin we've had a further request for further documents that Mr. Ackerman doesn't have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not sure exactly how many they are at the moment, and I'm not sure exactly to which witness they relate. I think -- I appreciate the difficulty. Mr. Ackerman has been working for the large part over this case on his own with very little assistance. It's been a difficulty for him. I'm well aware of that. But I think it may help, rather than this piecemeal request, if Mr. Ackerman could check through the various lists of documents for which he has signed receipts to see what he now says he's missing. Your Honour, as I said, it's not that simple a job to re-extract the documents, to redisclose them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we postpone this until Wednesday, Mr. Ackerman? In the meantime, perhaps you would have received the other documents that you have asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. There's no reason to take any of that up at the present time. The problem, and I'll just explain it so that maybe the Court will appreciate it, there are thousands and thousands and thousands and thousands of pages of documents. I think we're up around 100.000, somewhere in that neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It has gone down to half of what I was told initially during the first Pre-Trial Conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Maybe it's even more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At that time it was 200.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Whatever it is - and I just haven't counted lately - it's an extraordinary amount. And for me to take the time to sit down and see if I have every document that is on the Prosecution's list will mean that we can't possibly start this trial for another two or three weeks because I'll be doing that exclusively. The only thing I can do is, as I get from the Prosecution the list of exhibits they intend to use over the next three or four weeks, is go through that list as rapidly as I can and make sure I have them. It's complicated by the fact that I made a tactical error two years ago when I started cataloguing these documents, and that was I thought the ERN numbers that are on them were of no significance since the Prosecutor was putting their own numbers on them. So they're all catalogued by that number. And then when I say I need document such and such that's part of 7.163, they say, "Well, give us the ERN number." Well, you know, that takes me an hour to try to find out what the ERN number might be. So, you know, it's a big issue. The other thing, it's -- Ms. Korner just told you how difficult it is for them to retrieve and resupply a document they believe they've already supplied, and that just tells you how difficult it is for me to go through the process of trying to find these documents to see if I have them. And what I'm doing is I'm proceeding as rapidly as I can through them. I will have some additional help starting the end of this week. It's been approved to help me do that sort of thing, somebody who will actually manage documents for me, and then we can proceed a little faster, but I'm doing the best I can consistent with trying to get ready to cross-examine witnesses that are coming this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can assure you that I appreciate the difficulties that you each have, and you will find my cooperation. So we'll visit this problem again on Wednesday when we start the trial. And then possibly also as we go along, because what might apply to one witness might not apply to another. So if you are in agreement, we can, in the spirit of cooperation more than anything else and because it's more practical to approach it this way, we'll do it this way. Okay. There is then seventh motion from the Prosecution for additional protective measures. And before the Tribunal comes to a decision, I would like to know whether there is some sort of reaction from the Defence. This is a fairly recent motion, and I don't know if you have had time to file a response. I haven't come across any response from you as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will make an oral response right now. I have no objection to the request.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have none either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this will make the task of this Tribunal easy. This is, however, a motion which I will not decide orally. I will have a proper order issued in due course in terms of your request. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now we come to some or several very important aspects that we need to discuss here in preparation for the trial, and I would first mention a case management strategy. More or less, I think without needing to go into much detail, I understand that there is already an agreement on the part of the Prosecution to organise your case municipality by municipality. I have a confirmation of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. That's by and large light -- light -- right. There are obviously certain areas which cross over all municipalities; for example, expert testimony on religious destruction and the like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask you also with regard to the aspect of joint criminal enterprise whether you are -- you intend to tackle that or to bring evidence related to that particular aspect of the trial in the beginning or as you go along?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It really emerges as we go along. It comes from a number of witnesses who are in a position to deal with that and indeed from a number documents, in particular, the minutes of the various assembly minutes -- I'm sorry -- the minutes of the various assemblies that were held in the run-up to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, it's an aspect that I would imagine permeates the whole process and the whole -- all the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And therefore, you prefer or you intend to deal with it municipality by municipality as the case arises and as you need to prove the joint criminal enterprise arises.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. At the end of the evidence, we will be drawing together what we suggest is the evidence that there was a joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, I am going to suggest to you something which I think will be important and which I hope will meet with your agreement or your consensus. It is my suggestion to you, to smooth the proceedings that we will have to go through in the next 18 months, if not two years, that each time we are planning to move into a new municipality we will have, beforehand, a short Status Conference in preparation of what is intended to happen or is planned to happen for that or in that municipality phase of the trial. The whole idea is that what is really the raison d'etre behind the whole idea of a Status Conference for -- in the pre-trial stage will also be applied as a sort of a practice in the course and during the duration of the trial before we start each municipality. It will give us a chance to organise ourselves and, if necessary, the Tribunal will be prepared to give you all the time you need to organise yourselves in preparation of the new phase that will be approached, but we will do it together initially. Then after the Status Conference, the various Status Conferences I'm referring to, obviously you will have all the opportunities to organise yourselves. What is your response to this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we think that's an eminently sensible suggestion, if we may respectfully say so. The other matter that Your Honour may wish to examine in these short Status Conferences is whether the -- any facts that come out can be agreed in advance, and, for example, whether witnesses who the Prosecution intends to call, whether there is any part of their statements which can be led or summarised to shorten matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I will respond to that very quickly. In the meantime, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I also agree that that makes a great deal of sense, Your Honour. I think it will help us a lot, a good idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Defence counsel for Mr. Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree completely with your proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I am -- basically, I am very happy that this has gone down well with you. And in addition, may I just say or confirm to you that one of the ideas on having these Status Conferences held from time to time during the course of the trial is precisely what you have just mentioned. But in addition, I will be suggesting a system whereby on a weekly basis we will also visit these suggestions that you have made, Ms. Korner, and which will apply equally to the Office of the Prosecutor, perhaps more so than to the Defence at this particular stage of the trial, but I will come to that later. May I also deal with something which I consider very important, particularly for the proper running of this trial and for the whole concept of a fair trial in due process. I would not allow a situation whereby the Defence, as well as the Trial Chamber, are not aware as to the order in which witnesses will be called to testify. I understand that it is definitely the intention of the Prosecution to observe this cardinal rule, and the documentation that was handed to me last week precisely shows that that is the intention. But I want to make it clear that at all times and in real good time, the Defence should always be put in a position in which they know precisely the order which is going to be followed, so that they are in a position to prepare for due cross-examination and also to avoid the possibility of the Defence coming forward and saying, "We didn't know. We were not expecting this particular witness to give evidence now. We are not prepared for cross-examination now." So it is an understanding -- I'm not going to make any orders to this effect, but it is an understanding that this is the practice that will be followed by your office, Ms. Korner. Okay. Now, what I was going to suggest - and it's something that I hinted to barely a few minutes ago - is that -- and I also understand that this is a practice that has been applied by some other Judges in some other trials, although it's not a constant practice or a universal practice in this Tribunal. My suggestion to you is that every Thursday afternoon - give and take Thursday afternoon, because it could certain weeks be Friday or it could be Wednesday, depending on which week we may happen to find ourselves - but my suggestion to you is that on each Thursday afternoon, the Prosecution will file with the Registry a list of the witnesses it intends producing the following week. I don't think that would create big problems to the Prosecution because more or less you are always in a position to know which witnesses you're going to bring forward or you intend to bring forward the following week. Now, obviously there may -- I mean, this is not an absolute commitment, in the sense that you may find yourself faced with a witness that takes longer to testify and which would mean bringing one or two witnesses less the following week. But the whole idea is to have a clear picture of what the week ahead is likely to look like. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was only really rising because Your Honour was addressing me. But can I just mention two matters? The first is: Is it necessary to file it with the Registry, as opposed to, say, telling Your Honour and the Defence verbally?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. You can do that, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's just this place seems to exist on a glut of paperwork, and I would have thought anything less would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Anything identical or similar to the document that you were handed last Friday would be fine enough with me, and I would suppose that the Defence would not insist on the formality. I mentioned the formality because I wanted a reaction in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But Your Honour, may I just mention one thing? It, of course, is helpful if we can be given an indication in advance before we file this list how long cross-examination is likely to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's my next point, which I will address now to the Defence. The same applies to you, the Defence counsel. And although I'm sure that there will be some sort of reservations made, particularly at the early stages of the trial, I would invite you to be prepared to come along the same way and, if possible, confer with the Prosecution before this planning -- Thursday planning is made every week. It will only take you a few minutes, more or less. If there is this debate or dialogue going on between the two sides, you should be in a position to provide the Tribunal with a document, informal however it may be, that would make life easier for everyone. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, predicting - as you know, from having been in this business - predicting how long a cross-examination will take is really difficult because so much of what you do on cross-examination is dependent upon the kind of answers you get from the witness. A witness may give an answer that prolongs cross-examination by an hour or may give an answer that ends it at that exact moment. So you can't always predict it. What I would be able to do is give ballpark estimates, and with some witnesses, advise the Prosecution I don't intend to ask any questions at all. But that -- I'm perfectly willing to cooperate as much as I can, but just want to make sure if I tell the Prosecution it will take me an hour, that I'm not going to be told I can't ask any questions after that hour. That's the only thing I'm worried about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Madam Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We agree with what Mr. Ackerman said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So I take it that you agree also that there is going to be this ongoing dialogue between you, at least in this area of cooperation. Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. Your Honour, I certainly hope so. It will undoubtedly make things run a lot more smoothly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also, I would suggest that if this is the case and if that you anticipate that there not be major problems in this kind of cooperation, that you perhaps also from time to time try to -- in addition to this Thursday exercise, in other words, also give more or less general indication to the Prosecution of what your intended list of witnesses is for the forthcoming three weeks. In other words, more specifically for the following week, more generally with regard to the next three weeks. So it could be a month. It depends on which municipality we will be dealing with. I think if you follow that practice, I would anticipate more cooperation on the part of the Defence, and also you will be putting yourself in a stronger position if there are problems forthcoming from the Defence. I think it's also fair to enable the Tribunal to plan ahead and help you plan ahead a time schedule for this trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we certainly intend to do that, and it will be possible because we'll be warning witnesses in advance. I don't know whether Your Honour intends to at some stage revisit the overlap with the Stakic trial, because that does have an effect. And there is something I would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Basically, if you want me to stop here at this juncture on other things and discuss that, if it's that important to you, I would do so. Let me just tell you that first we're definitely not talking of any joinder issues between Stakic and this case. This case is going to start on Wednesday. And also, there is a problem with Stakic, as you know, because as the position stands to date, there are no funds readily available to make it possible for Stakic to start as the sixth ongoing trial for the moment. Of course, there are other matters that are pertinent to this trial and to Stakic which I would like to discuss with you in particular and also, of course, with the Defence counsel in this case, but I would prefer to have that done in a private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours -- I'm sorry. Your Honours, certainly, I quite understand. The only reason I raised it at this stage is because -- and can I emphasise there was never an application to join the two cases. We appreciated it was too late. And the ruling in fact merely dealt with that aspect of the matter. But I'm perfectly happy to deal with problems which are still extant at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't referring to any existing motion for joinder. I was just pre-empting the issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think we should go in private session now and discuss what Ms. Korner would like to raise in regard to Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are we in open session? Now, I'm -- I -- with regard to the exhibit lists, let me explain to you very briefly how I look at it, having worked in the jurisdiction of my own. I was trained, when I became a magistrate way back in 1977 in a jurisdiction where you don't study to become a Judge but you just -- like you have in your country. You receive no training beforehand, but then you have perhaps the best training for the bench, having come from the bar. And one practice that I had adopted with regard to exhibits was keeping a mind that the moment an exhibit becomes a document or an exhibit becomes an exhibit in a trial, it's no longer the party's document or exhibit but it's the case's exhibit or the Court's exhibit. I had various suggestions in this regard also because it seems that some problems have been encountered in the past, and what you said earlier on hints at that, that sometimes Defence find difficulties in keeping track of the documentation and the reference to documentation because it's a reference number which the Prosecution gives to its documents, et cetera. And it was suggested to me to change all this and to sort of provide for a system whereby the first exhibit that will be -- will be forthcoming will become P1 and then we continue P2, P3, et cetera, "P" meaning "Prosecution." Frankly, I have thought about it. I think it would create more problems than it would solve. What I am going to suggest is this: that each document or each exhibit that is produced in this trial, if it's produced or if it's forthcoming from the Prosecution, it will have a "P" added to it, either in front or at the back, so that it will always be distinguished as an exhibit of the Prosecution, forthcoming from the Prosecution. And similarly, an exhibit coming from the Defence will have an identification "D." If it's from defendant Brdjanin it will be "DB," and if it's defendant Talic, it will be "DT." I don't know if it's convenient for you, but it would be made easier later on for anyone that has to work with those exhibits to identify which is which. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I swear that I didn't have any anticipation of what you were going to say, Your Honour, but I have already for two years now numbered all of my documents not "DB" but "BD." So all of them have "BD." So if we go "BD" and "TD" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's -- that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- instead of the other way around, then I won't have to renumber anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem. Would you be agreeable to this, Madame Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no problem with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... There may also be cases where some documents will not be formally admitted, but they would still need to be marked for identification, and it has been suggested to me to have these designated by reference -- by the reference number that is given either by you or by the Defence and then identify them further by the addition of "MFI," whatever that means. I haven't had time to ask. But if you are in agreement with it, that's how it will be, and you are being told beforehand that "MFI" means -- it's not Malta Financial Institute but a document that is has not been -- okay. May I suggest to you, Ms. Korner, that as far as possible -- and it may not be always as convenient or useful for your case, but whenever is possible to have these exhibits organised municipality by municipality. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's been done. I was going to suggest that after the Court rises, we provide for Your Honours the copies of the Banja Luka municipality, plus the assembly minutes, which are ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this is what exactly I was coming to now, is the copies of the exhibits. So I don't need to touch upon that matter because it's being dealt with. We agreed that there will be five copies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We did, and there are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So the next thing to which I attach great importance, copies of witnesses' statements, copies of witnesses' statements. Let me tell you what system I would like to see in place. I did hint at something last Friday with regard to Rule 92 bis statements, et cetera. I wouldn't like to be flooded with documentation all at one go, which I would make -- create problems. The suggestion is to move municipality by municipality. But I would definitely like to have copies of any witness's statements beforehand. This is a practice that has been applied by at least two Judges that I have conferred with, and that's Judge Hunt and Judge May. They usually don't make an order -- and I'm not going to make an order to that effect, because I do not want to be too categorical in this or too demanding. I know that you may have problems. But where there are no problems, please do let me have copies of these statements beforehand because I always prefer to come here knowing, fully aware of what that witness had stated on previous occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no difficulty at all. We're delighted to provide Your Honours with copies of the statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I ask how far in advance of the witness being called, and would Your Honour like all the -- in some cases, witnesses have made statements earlier to, for example, authorities in Bosnia. Or merely the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me explain to you something. I told you last time when I was trying, actually, to defend the Defence teams, because of the difficulties that they encounter, that I never expect anyone to do two things at a time. So I realise that you are going to be fully occupied for several hours during the day with this trial. What I suggest you do - also because I am going to be fully equally occupied with this trial - is that in preparation of the production of a particular witness, you provide me realtime, at least, depending on how voluminous these statements would be. Use your good judgement. If we're talking of a witness who has given one statement which is only 20 pages long, then obviously, I mean, if it's given to me two days ahead, it's more than enough. If we're talking of a witness that has given multiple statements, and I run into hundreds of pages, that's no use giving it to me the day before because I will spend a restless and a sleepless night and I will definitely not be in the best of moods when I come for the trial the morning after. So use your good judgement. I mean, I have no reason to doubt your good judgement. You have shown it already in more than one instance. I have no reason to doubt your cooperation, because you have shown it all along. So I'm not going to give any orders. I'm just going to leave everything in your hands and in your good judgement. I mean, just don't flood me unnecessarily with a lot of documents weeks and months before. It doesn't make sense. Because what happened to Mr. Ackerman will probably happen to me, and I could easily lose track. It's better for me -- I mean, I have got a very efficient staff, both administrative and legal, that help me keep organised to the maximum and to the optimum on a daily basis. So if more or less -- I don't need much time, but I do need time to read them, because I am asking for them, because it's my intention to read them. So use your good judgement. I mean, more or less you should know. I mean, you're -- even your colleagues will tell you, I mean, "Mr. or Mrs. So and So will be giving evidence on Monday at -- I mean, we better hand it over straight away." Okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I take it that Your Honour doesn't mean just for Your Honour as the Presiding Judge but for your colleagues as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would imagine, yes. Yes, obviously. I mean, I have discussed a few things with the two Judges that will be flanking me during this trial. And perhaps if you have had the latest press release, you will know who they are. If you haven't, I will confirm -- I suppose your clients are not provided with press releases. But Mr. Brdjanin and General Talic, you know who I am; I am the Presiding Judge. The other two Judges are ad litem Judges. One is Judge Janu, from the Czech Republic; and the other is Judge Taya, from Japan. These are the two Judges that have been assigned to be with me in this Trial Chamber for the purposes of this trial. Thank you. The same applies to any Rule 92 bis statements that have not been already made available. I mean, I -- we discussed this more or less, the 72 witnesses, 75 witnesses that you intend to apply. So again, as we go along, please --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'd suggest is it would have to be in advance of the evidence from the municipalities starting but on one of our Thursday, as it were, discussions, because clearly we need to know well in advance which witnesses we will be allowed to use -- deal with under Rule 92.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also with regard to the Thursday afternoon exercise, if there is going to be a dialogue between you - and it's something that I suggested - perhaps I could offer you either the assistance of a senior legal officer to coordinate with you whatever needs to be coordinated. Obviously, I mean, it will be -- even my assistance and that of my other Judges in this Chamber, if necessary. So if there are difficulties and you need or you would find -- think that it will be more useful even to meet in my Chambers informally to organise things always ahead of -- programming ahead, I am offering you my cooperation. I've discussed this also with the other two Judges, and they would of course come along with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course we're not sitting in the afternoons for the next few weeks. We finish at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think Your Honour has heard of some of the difficulties we've had in getting together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think it would be extremely helpful if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And I think -- listen, I mean, I have enough experience in this. I also know that once the trial starts, the atmosphere changes as well. There will be new terrain for you to -- to engage and to combat, but also there will be -- there will also be ground for -- and need to come forward and meet halfway on many issues. I'm offering you my services if you need them, in the way which they state -- the Rules permit and within those parameters. And if that can be helpful -- I think it's very important to have this trial start and move ahead in the right environment. It's -- the atmosphere. I'm not saying that I do not expect fireworks, that I expect everything to work like a Swiss clock or watch. I mean, no trial does. But please do allow me to interfere and intervene when necessary to bring it together and move ahead as required. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a request with regard to the Rule 92 bis issue, because I think it's just a practical way to deal with it. The Prosecutor, as you know, filed this list of the Banja Luka witnesses and included, I think, four Rule 92 bis proposals in that list. And it was very easy for me to take the four of those and respond to them, and I filed what I call document number 1. If that could be the procedure that I am permitted to follow in the future, it would -- I think it makes sense. So that when the Prosecutor gives us a list and gives us the Rule 92 bis things, I will at that point respond rather immediately to those, rather than trying to do all of the Rule 92 bis things at once, which I could do, but I would simply have to take a couple or three days off my trial preparation to get that done, for no good purpose, because I'd probably change my mind sometime later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Actually, you did at one time, when you raised the issue of the presiding officer. You attacked all 92 bis. So Ms. Korner, do you have any particular objection to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I do not, Your Honour. If I may say so, it seems very sensible. As I said, we'll notify the Defence and Your Honour with the lists for the municipalities who we'd wish to call as Rule 92 witnesses. The only thing is that, as Your Honour knows, I suggested to Your Honour that once the trial starts, we could stop this endless proliferation of written motions. But I think that's probably -- for those purposes, it's more sensible. If we all get it in writing, we can then deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We did mention something last time also that particular objections, motions will be raised orally and will be decided orally. I mean, this is something that I was reading again -- when I was reading again the transcript of last Friday's hearing, this is something that we have made clear. This is the practice that I would like you to follow. It makes sense. Okay? So copies of witness statements we have. Now, I am going to revisit a very important matter that we touched upon during the 10th December Pre-Trial Conference hearing, when it was suggested to the Prosecution to adopt the practice for this particular trial of preparing witness testimony sheets.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I think there was some confusion there, or at least between us. Was it, Your Honour I thought may have been referring to the practice that was adopted whereby if a witness was going to refer to another witness who was protected, then he should do -- he should be given a sheet showing what that witness, who had been protected, his pseudonym was. I know that Judge Hunt followed it in the Vasiljevic case. The point was made to me that in fact if the witness is protected from -- and the protection is from public identification, then a witness referring to another witness who has been given a pseudonym, by that pseudonym tends more rather to identify him than if that name is just mentioned, because the public won't know it. I have to say, though, I'm not aware of how successfully or not it worked in the Vasiljevic case. It's safe to say that it was a much more limited case and there wasn't the same repetition, I think, of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me explain to you -- because this was something that was suggested to me by my legal officers and which has engaged me in -- to some towards. Let me tell you what the practical problems -- You may sit down, Ms. Korner. Let me tell you what the practical problems that I envisage are. First of all, there is the practical problem of having a witness taking the stand and starting to give evidence and either unwittingly or because for some other reason, the name of another witness who may be protected is disclosed. The suggestion is that before a witness starts giving evidence, he or she is handed a list showing the names and pseudonyms of protected witnesses, so that if it is the intention of that witness to refer to any of those protected witnesses, he will be forewarned and foreadvised how to deal with that. In other words, that witness will be told at the very beginning, "You will not refer to Mr. So and So by his name but by his particular pseudonym." Ideally it's a good approach, but I see an inherent danger, because I also would imagine that that particular witness might not be aware of the various or all of all the persons that are going to be giving evidence in the trial and that list would reveal to him or to her names otherwise -- that could otherwise remain unknown to him or to her. That is the only practical problem that I see. Is there a solution to it? I think there might be a solution. One way of dealing with it - I was thinking about it last night - was that perhaps in the beginning of the evidence or before the witness actually starts to give evidence, he or she is told or asked whether in the course of the evidence he or she is going to make reference or mention any particular persons. This will be done in closed session, so that if the witness is going to refer to particular persons by name, we would know beforehand and we would be able to tell him or her, tell the witness, "Listen, if you're going to refer to Mr. So and So, you will never refer to that person by Mr. So and So but you will refer to that person by this pseudonym," and so on and so forth. That could be one alternative approach. In other words, the names of the persons will be forthcoming from the -- that the witness intends to refer to or mention would be coming -- forthcoming from the witness. That would not definitely be the case of disclosing to the witness other names. And there is also another problem -- practical problems that I envisage: That I see from past experience that a witness that is -- in favour of whom there is no protective order as yet might eventually turn up and ask for a protective order immediately before giving evidence. So how do we go about this problem? Frankly, I don't know. If you have any practical suggestions to me, please do come forward.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, firstly, there are many problems from this particular method. One is that the witness in advance doesn't tell you that he's going to talk -- it's not in his statement, and he doesn't tell you he's going to talk about somebody who is protected, and in chief or in cross-examination it comes up without any warning. Your Honour, with the greatest respect, I actually don't think that this type of thing is necessary, and I think it's going to make life too complicated and difficult for the witnesses themselves if they're trying to remember and all the rest, even with a sheet of paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know it's definitely not easy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only -- the witnesses themselves who are protected are protected to the extent that their names are not revealed to the public, they're given a pseudonym, or in some cases they're testifying in closed session or with the other measures. The fact that a witness is going to mention witnesses -- other witnesses who may have given evidence or who will be giving evidence with protection doesn't matter, provided he doesn't say that that witness has testified or will testify. That's the only problem. And provided, if necessary, he's warned, that's all that's needed. Your Honour, I -- with the greatest respect, in a case of this size, and in many cases where witnesses will be talking about not just one incident but multiple incidents, it will, I think, cause unnecessary problems. And so with the greatest of respect, as I say, I know it was used in the Vasiljevic case. That was effectively --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm raising it because it has been used. I actually am very hesitant myself in recommending it because I see inherent dangers and also I see the practical problems that it brings up. But since it has been used in other trials and since we mentioned it or I mentioned it in the 10 December hearing, and there was no negative reaction on that occasion but we had agreed to revisit it later on -- I mean, I wanted to hear what your opinion is. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm familiar that at least one Trial Chamber got confused about this matter. And I think -- I think we ought not to get into that. There is absolutely no mischief, as Ms. Korner pointed out, in a witness saying, "I was at a certain place in a certain time in 1992 and I either saw or had a conversation with Joe Smith," if Joe Smith is going to be a witness in the case. I mean, it's just not a problem --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- at all. The only problem is -- and I understand Joe Smith will be coming here to testify next week. That's the problem. And so that's what we're trying to avoid. But to try to say to each witness, "You must never say the name of a person who is or might be a witness in this case," just overly complicates everything. It's a identification of that person as witness that's the the problem, not the identification of that person as someone who was there in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the issue has been sufficiently clarified by Mr. Ackerman and Madam Korner, and I quite agree with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll deal with problems that may arise as we go along, but it's been agreed that this will not be -- this system will not be adopted in this particular case unless it is needed -- any particular witness is giving evidence or before a particular witness is giving evidence, if we see inherent danger there or risk. Last time you asked me whether I was going to deny you the opening statement. Of course not. But I want to know how long you anticipate it will last.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It wasn't that I thought Your Honour was going to deny it to me. There just didn't seem to be any room for it. Your Honour, as best I can, and I haven't yet completed my notes on this, I would think with the breaks it's likely to take, if not all of Wednesday morning of the time allotted, the best part. So I would ask even if I finish a little earlier that we say that Dr. Donia doesn't start, as agreed, until the Thursday morning. But I think it will because it's of course having to speak quite slowly for the translation and will take the best part of the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ackerman and Ms. Fauveau, you know that you have as an option also the possibility of making a opening statement immediately after the Prosecutor's opening statement. That's one option that you have. For the moment, I'm addressing you as Defence counsel. Is it your intention -- may I ask you if it is your intention to make such a statement immediately after?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will open at the beginning of the Defence case, Your Honour, if there is one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will also be making our opening statement at the beginning of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now as you know, there is another option... Ready for a break? Let me put this question and we'll break for 20 minutes. There is also another option which the -- our Rules make available to the two defendants, and actually, the Chamber will be asking the two defendants in due course when we start the trial whether they would like to make -- themselves to make a statement. I am not going to ask them myself now, but perhaps I could ask each one of you to confer with your client and at least put me in a position to know whether to expect -- the question will be asked, in any case, on Wednesday or on Thursday when we come to that stage, but I would like to know beforehand, if possible, whether it is expected -- I am to expect your clients to make a statement at the beginning of the trial. Mr. Ackerman, perhaps if you already know the answer, you could tell me, but I wouldn't like to put the question directly to your clients myself. I'm asking you to confer with them if -- if that is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will confer with my client.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will also confer with my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you will give me a reply immediately after the coffee break. Thank you. We'll break for 20 minutes. We are doing fine. Twenty, 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Welcome back. A piece of good information: The B/C/S translation of the indictment is ready and will be made available to you in the course of today's business. So that solves one problem. Before we had the break, we agreed that you will confer with your respective clients and tell me whether to expect an opening statement from them. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My client will not make a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My client will not be making a statement either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, on that topic of defendants -- accused testifying, may I just raise at this stage for Your Honours consideration one aspect? In the jurisdiction in which Your Honour practices and certainly in England and Wales, if the defendant is to testify, he must do so before any other witnesses that are called. Your Honour, the practice isn't as clear in this Tribunal, and I wondered whether Your Honour would say that that is a matter that Your Honour will consider at an appropriate time when the Defence case, if there is a Defence case, starts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is not a matter that I have discussed with the other two Judges. I have discussed with the other two Judges some other matters that I will communicate to you before the trial starts, such as the practice that will be followed by this Chamber with regard to leading questions, for example. Also because I understand that there has been a practice which has not been common to all Judges and all Chambers, it has been dealt with differently in different instances, and I think you ought to know the way I will deal with this problem. This other matter I promise you I will discuss with Judges Janu and Taya before the trial begins, and either on the first day of the trial or at some point in time, I will let you know what is going to happen. In my jurisdiction, as you say, that's the practice. So I will also discuss the matter with some of the other Judges to see how it has been dealt with in the past. Thank you for bringing that to my attention. Future motions. I think we agreed last time, and it was also mentioned earlier on today, that as far as possible once the trial has started, then applications that may become necessary or that you would deem you need to make should be made orally as much as possible, with a skeleton argument in advance, and wherever possible and desirable, the decisions will be taken orally as well. Obviously they will be recorded as everything else, but they will be taken orally. We come to something which is very important: trial schedule. I told you the very first time that I met you in December that I'm fully aware this is a long trial, by no means an easy trial. It's a trial that, if not conducted as it should be, could give rise to many problems, one problem in particular being getting one or more of us tired or unduly tired. Though it's not my intention to use pressure on either the Defence or the Prosecution, it is, rather, my intention to expect -- to be very frank with you and also to expect you to be very frank with the Chamber and if there are problems, to let me know. This would necessitate from the very first go a careful scheduling of the hearing. I invite you not to give too much attention to what you have seen in the various Tribunal schedule that was circulated, in other words, not to expect the Chamber to sit in this particular case from now until the end of March precisely and infallibly and necessarily on all those days that are indicated or for the time that are indicated. I would, before I go any further on this matter, like to hear what you have to say. Tell me what your preferences are, although these need not -- may not necessarily coincide with what I have in mind. Shall I start with you, Ms. Korner? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have at present arranged a witness schedule, working on the basis of the court schedule, in other words, that bar two mornings, one for maintenance and one for the UN holiday, we would be sitting. Of course, it is entirely a matter for the Court to decide. All we would ask is perhaps some warning in advance, because of bringing witnesses from the various countries in which they reside. It is very difficult, obviously. And I'm conscious of what Mr. Ackerman said to Your Honour in December about his practice in the United States. However, it would be the Prosecution preference, given as Your Honour says that it's a long trial, to proceed on a basis of a virtual daily sitting with odd days maybe. Otherwise we may well be here for years. But as I say, in the end result, it's a matter for the Chamber to decide what days we sit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is true. But what I want to say is if you have -- what I want to know is if you have any particular requests that you would like to air at this present moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: None at all, Your Honour, except that the trial proceed fairly regularly, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. That is the intention of the Chamber as well. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I believe I said at the last time we discussed this that I was hoping that the Chamber would hit upon a schedule that involved sessions of approximately four weeks with a week break, which would enable me to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Initially, you said two weeks. And then I corrected you and put you back on track, and I said we can't work two weeks on and two weeks off. I mean, that would ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that was contemplating full time in court, which is what we did in another case that I was involved in. But a four-week schedule with a week off would give me an opportunity to take care of matters in the United States that I need to take care of. And not -- not a small concern about that is that I have a wife and family there. And it's very difficult, the separation -- the long separation is very difficult. The other thing that I would mention to you is that Mr. Brdjanin's wife and family try to visit him with some frequency. And he must make arrangements a month in advance of those visits. Based upon a schedule that was floating around here in the last several days, it -- the schedule indicated that there would be a break in this case between the 22nd of January -- 22nd of February and the 4th of March. And based upon that, Mr. Brdjanin scheduled a visit with his wife during that -- that week. And we believed that that was the schedule that would be adhered to. I've also informed my wife that I would be coming home at that time and informed a co-counsel in another case that that would be an appropriate time to set that case for a hearing in Galveston, Texas. And if that's not to be the case, then some changes need to be made rather Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. quickly with regard to all of those matters. But I would hope --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 22nd February to ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: March 4. That was a schedule that was in existence and floating around the Tribunal. And, you know, I would not have -- neither of us would have made any of those kinds of arrangements had we not seen that schedule, of course. And I didn't see it. I was just told that that's what it said. But in any event, I would hope that we could adhere to a schedule somewhere along -- something along that line. I wouldn't mind a five-week session now and then if we need to move things. But as I told you the last time we discussed this, I think if you try to move too rapidly, you'd lose efficiency and wind up spending time that wouldn't really need to be spent if lawyers were less tired and more prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do I also take it that your presence is required elsewhere on the 11th and the 12th of February?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I should have mentioned that. Yes. I'm supposed to be in Sarajevo on those two days. And it's rather important, I think, that I be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Let me hear Madam Fauveau first, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be brief. It seems to me that it is indispensable for us who don't live here in The Hague and have an office elsewhere, family elsewhere too, we must have a specific schedule. But I would also like to say that it might be worth thinking about having a break between the various municipalities. Because if the Prosecutor gives us a list of exhibits a few days in advance -- and we received the list last Wednesday with 600 exhibits in it. We've got to go through them. We've got to collate it. We've got to look through them. We're going to need a break in order to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First on Mr. Ackerman's schedule. I think the error -- I don't think there was ever a schedule published showing that break, but it could be, if you don't look at it carefully enough, it could look as though there was a break of a week, because I made that mistake at first until I had another look at it. The difficulty is, of course, everyone has professional responsibilities. We all understand that. But as I understood it, the idea of co-counsel is that if one counsel can't be here, another one can take over, and that -- in order to prevent breaks where we have professional commitments. I, as it turns out, have a professional commitment on the Monday, the 5th of February in England arising out of a case I did many years ago, but other people can take over so I'm not asking for any break there. Mr. Ackerman would like to see his wife and children. Equally I would like to go back to England to take up my practice in England, but Your Honour, it one has a commitment to a case, it seems to me that considerations have to be secondary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's beyond question. I mean, that is definitely the main consideration that we should keep in mind, that the involvement of each and every one in this case is not something that has been imposed against your will, but it is something that you have. You have duties, responsibilities, and we have to work with that assumption first, under that assumption first. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it is right to say that these accused, through no fault of anybody, really, through the lack of courts, have been waiting a long time for the trial and to extend it unnecessarily by perhaps unnecessary breaks - obviously there must be breaks - is not terribly helpful. Your Honour, that's really all I want to say on the matter except on, as it were, a side note, I don't know whether Your Honour has in mind any sort of curtailment, arbitrary curtailment in one sense, of evidence, either in chief or in cross, but if so, it would be something that I'd wish to know about at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but -- exactly. That's why I wanted more information from you, because it's -- I find it very undesirable to pronounce myself or even consider that possibility without first going into details. I mean, for example, let's -- between the option of telling you, as has happened in other instances, I don't want Mr. Donia to give evidence on historical events, because what I am interested in is what happened since 1991 and not before. I would rather let you have your -- the space necessary to prepare your case and to bring it forward and then regulate the matter as we go along. That's my system. I mean, I don't like to preempt issues beforehand, always beforehand, if I am pre-empting, but in any case, there may be instances whereas we go along, it becomes obvious that you don't need a particular witness or a number of witnesses if what they are going to confirm is something that has already been confirmed more than enough by previous witnesses. I think we have to take it as we go along, but I will try to create the least inconvenience to you and to Defence as possible. But don't expect me to tell you beforehand, going through the whole list of a trial that is expected to last two years, that I'm going to curtail on this. I will be curtailing, definitely. I mean, every Judge does in every trial, but as we go along, as we go along. And I will give you an indication. You know, I mean, it's ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's start from this. We are going to start on the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically let's start from here: We'll start on the 23rd, and then I think without needing to explain why Mr. Ackerman is needed in Sarajevo on the 11th and the 12th of March -- of February -- of February, correct? I am informed of the circumstances, and I think it's only fair to make an allowance for that. On the 8th of February, I need to be elsewhere myself. So basically I would suggest that we hold sittings right through from the 23rd of January to the 7th of February to start with, without interruptions, then stop from the 8th. Do you think, Mr. Ackerman, you will return on the 13th or you would prefer to resume on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I can resume on the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I can resume on the 13th, if Your Honour wishes. I can leave Sarajevo rather early, I think, on the 12th and be prepared for that if you'd like. If it's more convenient, I'll wait until the 14th, but I will struggle to make -- I know this is personal privilege I'm asking for here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's something that the Tribunal is -- I personally and the Tribunal -- I haven't discussed it with the other two Judges because it came upon me unexpectedly, but I'm sure the other two Judges will agree with my decision. I think I have absolutely no problems in meeting you on this and granting permission. I think it's important.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll plan to resume on the 13th unless I have indications that this would be better it resume on the 14th. But definitely it will be either the 13th or the 14th. For the moment, it's the 13th. Then we will sit right through -- I don't think at this point in time, Mr. Ackerman, that I can stop again for nine days, from the 22nd of February to the 3rd of March. I think at this point in time, we have to reschedule, making it possible for your client to make the necessary arrangements for his consort to visit him, but I don't think we can stick to those days, I mean, which -- I mean, I never got the impression from the time schedule that I had that this was intended to be a break. I mean, I never got -- I went through that schedule very carefully and I never got this impression. I mean, I may have been wrong, but I didn't see it anyway. So we would sit right through from the -- let's make it more feasible straight away. Rather than restarting on the 13th, we will start on the 14th, on the 14th, and we will sit right through - one, two, three - right through -- now, you tell me whether we prefer -- you prefer right through Friday the 8th of March or Friday the 15th of March. And then we will have a break. Tell me what your preferences are.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm trying to remember when Easter is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Easter is the 31st of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's the 31st of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It's coming pretty early this year.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So Your Honour is deciding on a break either the 7th or the 14th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Either -- yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: For how long?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For a week. I mean, I don't know. If you want more, I'll give you more, but -- if you need more, I will give you more, but I don't think we ought to break for more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want less. I'd like to sit all the way through, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At that point in time, Madam Korner, you will probably need a week because we will be approaching the end of Banja Luka, and you will probably need some time to -- I don't know. It's my expectation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know the list of exhibits will be provided to the Defence much more in advance than it was before, but, Your Honour, as far as our preference is concerned, Your Honour, I would have to go back and look at the list of -- at the moment, we have witnesses coming solidly between the beginning of the trial and the end of March. So I would need to check on how best to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Normally it's not the practice of this Court, of this Tribunal, to recess for what in my country we'd call Holy Week, Easter recess. There is no Easter recess here, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good Friday is a holiday, and I understand -- is Easter? I believe Easter Monday. Yes. I think if Your Honour were to say what would be the preference for all of us, we would prefer to have the break either in the week running up to Easter or after Easter, because everyone with families and schools would prefer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll break on the -- okay. That could make life easier for everyone. We could break after the 21st of March. Is that -- am I reading you well?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right through the 2nd of April, because Monday would be a holiday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that agreeable with you, Mr. Ackerman, and Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With all respect, Your Honour, that's an awfully long time. I left Texas right after the 1st of January. That's almost three months. And there's a judge in Galveston that, among other things, will not be happy with that but a wife who will be even less happy, and family. I really think the 8th of March is a more reasonable time. I'd be happy to accommodate you on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If we recess at the 8th of March, I can't give you a whole week then, because then comes Easter and we have to stop for Easter again, and someone will come forward with ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should say that by the 8th of March, we certainly won't be nearing the end with the break in February of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, you definitely won't. No, definitely not. Definitely not. Listen, Mr. Ackerman, if we break on the 22nd of March, there you have 11 days, which will be a much better deal than if you -- if we break a week earlier. You know, I mean, because I myself had suggested the 8th or the 15th. If we break on the 15th, you're not going to have 11 days or 12 days. I mean, if we break on the 22nd, you're going to have 11 days, possibly even 12 if we stretch it a little bit, and that would also coincide with more or less the conclusion on -- of the Banja Luka chapter. I invite you to consider it. I mean, I -- I don't like imposing in these things. And you are realising that I don't. But I would seriously invite you to consider this option, because I think it's -- it makes you meet halfway. In other words, it would not create -- it would not be embarrassing for the Tribunal, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Based, Your Honour, upon the proposition that the transcript of this proceeding is a public document, it would not be wise for me to consent. But I can say that it's up to you to set the schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Madam Fauveau, I know that your other two partners are not here, and I wouldn't dare say what their preferences will be, but I suppose that you are here and fully briefed and you can help me with making some concrete suggestions in this direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I defer to the Tribunal completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So let's go back. We start on the 23rd, break from the 8th till the 13th, recommence on the 14th, right through the 21st, then break from the 22nd -- I gave you an extra day now -- break from the 22nd till April 1st, resuming on April the 2nd. In any case, I wouldn't have liked to resume on April 1st because I don't know whether you would have taken me seriously. Now, I think for the moment we can leave it at that and take up the matter of rescheduling for post-April later on. Okay? Also because no one exactly knows what will come up between now and then. If we need to amend this or change this, please advise me beforehand, particularly not because of me and my commitment but because of what Mr. Ackerman has mentioned. I mean, I would like to cooperate in these matters as much as possible and make sure that defendants do not suffer any undue inconveniences. There is one other thing that I need to tell you. In discussing a few things with Judge Janu, in view of the fact that she has now been nominated as an Ad Litem Judge in this case, she will -- she needs to resign from her post in her office as the vice-president of the constitutional court of the Czech Republic, or she has decided to do that, something that she could keep for the time being, considering that she had only the Vasiljevic case. And this may necessitate her presence in Prague for one or more days in February. The dates will depend on the President of the Czech Republic, and she has no control. And she has informed me about this, and I said, "Once you know the days, then" -- but I will be informing her on the dates when we will be, in any case, stopping so that she will try to possibly make the visit to the President of the Czech Republic to coincide with those dates. That's something that I can't promise, something she hasn't got much control upon, in any case, because it depends on the President's agenda. But I thought it fair to forewarn you or inform you about this beforehand. Otherwise, I don't think there should or ought to be any problems. I'll just repeat what I told you before.
