There may be times when you may have problems, when you feel tired, when the case is taking its toll on you or on me. Please be frank. Do let me know. I would rather prefer that we work on this matter and in this context rather than through other means or other matters. So that's sorted out. Are there any other matters that either the Prosecution or the Defence would like to raise at this point before we conclude?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a number of matters. Quite short ones, I hope. First of all, can I invite Your Honour to look at the list of witnesses that was supplied to the Court last week. And if I can find my own copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I gave it to my secretary to have it filed this morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I've got it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But anyway, I ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in relation to witness on that list numbered 7.177, Witness number 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I need a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can hand Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because my secretary has it for filing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- my copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness number?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 7.177, I think I said number 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has been contacted twice and declines to attend. He is a journalist. Can I hand Your Honour at this stage a copy of his statement - it's very short - and the article which is the subject of his testimony. Your Honour, I don't need Your Honour to read it at the moment because there are two options. One is that we apply to Your Honour, which we do now, if necessary, for a witness summons. And there are various complications attached to the service of that summons because of the country in which he resides. The only topic -- the reason for declining is one that Your Honour will be no doubt familiar with. It's the journalistic reluctance to testify. The only evidence he's going to give is in relation to that article, which all can read. What I am raising it for at this moment is if that article is accepted in evidence, there's no requirement for the witness to attend. And that's the reason I'm raising it now. If there is a requirement for this witness to attend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does the Defence have a copy of this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This has all been disclosed, yes. If it is required for the witness to attend, then we'll have to ask Your Honour to issue a summons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: More or less, before I make any comments on this, given that you will respect the order of witnesses, as indicated in this document, and this witness being number 14, when would you anticipate him to be present in this courtroom between now and March?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: With the breaks Your Honour has now given, I'd have to recalculate. Your Honour now has my list, so I can't see the ones who are in advance, but I would have thought sometime in March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can say, Your Honour, I don't think it affects General Talic at all. It's only evidence in respect of Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman, do you recall this document, or do you require time to locate it in the 100.000 pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If responded now, it would be very simple. And that is I would absolutely oppose anything that would involve his article coming into evidence without his being subject to cross-examination. I think he -- I think he is easily subpoenaed or summoned. If he's important to the Prosecution, that's what they should do. Newspaper articles, as a practical matter, are notoriously unreliable, should not be admitted in evidence ever for any purpose that would -- a purpose that would tend to try to prove a fact at issue in the case. If you want to put a newspaper in evidence to show that it was raining on a certain day or that it was cold on a certain day or something like that, or a stock price was a certain price, that's one matter. But I can -- I can show Your Honour how unreliable newspaper articles are. There is a newspaper here from, I think, last week which has a photograph -- it's about the start of this trial. It has a photograph on it of a person who the newspaper identifies as General Momir Talic. And if one tried to use this newspaper to prove that that's General Momir Talic, a huge injustice would occur, because it's actually Mr. Brdjanin. And that's the kind of thing that you encounter all the time in newspapers. And I might as well raise it now. I object to the use of any newspaper articles to prove a fact at issue in this case. And this one falls in that same position. And it may very well be that this person doesn't want to come because they can't substantiate what they wrote in the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, this witness statement that you've shown me, it's purported to have been signed. Has it been signed by --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The one I have here is definitely not signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, because it's a typed copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, that's your answer. In other words, you don't require time. You're not asking for time to go any further in this matter, you're just telling the Tribunal -- the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I would leave -- I would certainly leave open the possibility. Once I go look at it, I will then say to the Court I will stipulate to the fact contained therein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, because what you actually said with regard to the probative value of newspaper articles, et cetera -- I mean, I think what you said is what I know and what everyone else knows, and I don't think that the Prosecution is asking to produce Mr. -- whoever it is as a witness or his article because the whole case is going to depend entirely on this article. I mean, it's an article like many other articles. It may have probative value; it may not have probative value. I think I will read it myself. In the meantime, please go into it. If you require the details, the reference number, I will give it to you. Okay. I will take a decision later on. I mean, I wanted to know how early you intend -- you would have intended to produce this person, this witness, simply because I wanted to know how much time I need to devote to it. You know what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse. I'd like to go back to the article. I want to make sure that this has no effect on General Talic's case. So I'll give an answer as soon as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would have asked you for your reaction in any case, but it seems that it does not involve your client in the least, at least at face value.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only reason that we ask for a ruling or a decision from Mr. Ackerman fairly early on - and, Your Honour, this is an interview conducted by the journalist with Mr. Brdjanin - is that if it is necessary to issue a subpoena, the country in which the witness resides, the procedures are a bit more complicated. It's not, unfortunately, just a matter of Your Honour issuing it and them complying. Your Honour, that's the first matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will deal with that straight away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Your Honour, the second matter is this: The -- in a couple of cases, an issue was raised by Defence counsel as to what in generic terms could be called assistance to witnesses by the Office of the Prosecutor. For example, if a witness is residing in a country as a refugee, a letter is sent saying that the person is a witness and the OTP would prefer that the witness remains in a country or wherever it is, and there are other odd instances. If it is thought to be of any relevance to any issue in this trial, then the Office of the Prosecutor is happy to supply the Defence with details of any witnesses that have received such assistance, but it was raised certainly in the trial involving the Keraterm camp and, I believe, one other trial. So I'm just, as it were, pre-empting the matter to say if that's what's required, if it's thought to be of assistance, then the Prosecution is happy to provide those details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it depends on the nature of the assistance, Your Honour. It sometimes can go very directly to witness bias. And now that Ms. Korner has raised this, I'm involved in trying to determine now whether or not some information I received is correct, and I'm not going to go beyond saying that I have received information that the Prosecutor is in fact paying people in Bosnia to speak with them, which I think would just be outrageous if that is the case, if they actually -- when they go to interview someone if they're giving them money in exchange for them cooperating with the Prosecutor. I think that would be -- that's the kind of thing that could just throw this whole case into complete chaos. And I seriously doubt that's happening. I have some indication and we're conducting an investigation into it, and I may or may not raise it at a later time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would have raised it at a time when the information that you have is more substantive and more substantial than the one you have now, because it's a very serious accusation, and if you are not in a position to substantiate your accusation, I would prefer -- rather prefer not to raise it. I don't know if you want to react to this, but I don't think there is place for any reaction on your part--

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- because it is just a gratuitous assertion at this point in time to which I wouldn't respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Mr. Ackerman wants to present us with any evidence, we'll be happy to look into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anything --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing to add on this point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I made the offer and if anybody wants to take me up on it, it is there. Your Honour, I think then the only other matter that I want to raise is this, and it's really a question of trial management: As I explained to Your Honour, the witness immediately following Dr. Donia will be the lead investigator who has prepared a schedule of the documents that are going to be used in this case, as to where they come from and the like, and I'm proposing to put him in the witness box. I imagine just -- we will have to deal with this in chunks, but so that he can explain to Your Honour the general system and deal with any disputes as to admissibility that Your Honour has already alluded to. Mr. Ackerman has very helpfully supplied us over the weekend with, and I think it's a rolling list of documents contained in the Banja Luka folders to which he will be taking objection, and, therefore, we hope to deal with those on whichever day Mr. Inayat testifies. You will recall last time I attempted to persuade Your Honour that counsel for Talic should do the same thing, they having declined. Your Honour, I raise it now only for this reason: that clearly if there is going to be an in-depth examination of any -- of some or more documents, the investigator will have to say, "Well, I'll have to go back and check on that because this is -- you haven't raised this before, and I'll have to go and check on other records that we have." In order to try and keep this trial running smoothly, Your Honour may think it would be of assistance if counsel for General Talic could adopt the same attitude as Mr. Ackerman and let us know in advance - I anticipate he will be given evidence sometime next week - which documents are going to be the subject of dispute as to authenticity and/or admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that Mr. Pitron has already explained, and I cannot be clearer than he has been. There are three types of documents that we can contest. They are documents signed by General Talic, signed by him, and I haven't yet found a single one that is being contested, which doesn't mean to say that I might not find a document that may appear to have been signed by General Talic and that we will contest. But for the moment, all the documents are carrying handwritten signatures by General Talic are not contested. What we tried to explain was that there are a certain number of documents on which there is the typed name of General Talic, but in handwriting there is the word "za," which in Serbo-Croatian means "for," therefore, it is clear that they were not signed by General Talic. And in our pre-trial brief and also in the request for agreement, she refers -- the Prosecutor refers to these documents. It is sufficient to read them, so I don't see why we should provide such a list to the Prosecutor. And the third group of documents are documents that are not signed by anyone, that bear no stamp, and which is very difficult to authenticate. We are not going to contest that these documents were found, shall we say, in the Banja Luka municipality or in the security centre in Banja Luka, but the fact that they were found there doesn't mean to say that they were written by our client. But it is very easy to find them because those documents bear no signature and no stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically, I think, Ms. Korner, you have to live with this problem. It's not going to be easy. And much of what Madam Fauveau has just said has a lot of truth and a lot of reality in it. I mean, I think we will have to move -- not exactly play it by the ear, but we have to move bit by bit and document by document as we go along. I think more or less we have identified an area to which this contestation is restricted, and that's with regard to the internationality of the conflict. If I remember well, that was -- that was one question that was raised by you last time, whether it's all the documentation relating to all the case, as broad as it is, or whether it is restricted within the parameters shown or at least purported to be shown in the documents you referred to last time. And I think we have identified at least that limitation and we have to move from there. I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't -- I think Your Honour is going to see the problem, but I think we'll have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can see it already.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I think we will have to, as Your Honour says rightly, play it by ear, and when Mr. Inayat starts to testify, then we'll see how this problem can be resolved. What would be highly undesirable, in our submission, would be if a witness turns up to testify and then is kept waiting or the evidence is stopped while we argue about a particular document, which is why I'm anxious to establish, before the witnesses come who are going to refer to these documents, whether or not they will be admitted or they will not be admitted, and I think that is why we need to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I also -- I mean, I can foresee some problems, definitely, but I also am trying to look at it with as practical an eye approach as possible. In reality, what do you have in each trial? You have the filing, the presentation of the document or of the exhibit by a particular individual, by a particular witness. That witness might be in a position to testify on that document, particular document, to a small or to a large extent, depending on how much he or she was involved in the procuring of that document. And the procuring of that document does not necessarily mean that he or she is in a position to testify on the content, because the content may be another matter which other witnesses will visit. So more or less you have first the question of the probative value of the document or of the contents of the document. Secondly, the authenticity. And the authenticity, I think you can sometimes have it -- have it dealt with in stages. I mean, the person who is exhibiting the document, who will just state, "This document, the origin of this document is the following," and would not be in a position to give any further information in regard to any allegation of non-authenticity that might be forthcoming. You may have the question of having to prove the authenticity. It depends. And sometimes you have an objection which is taken at superficial value as an objection and that's it. Sometimes you have to go deeper than that. I mean, it's -- I think we have to play it by the ear. But it's a problem that you are going to encounter. I'm sure you will find the Tribunal taking a very radical approach if at the moment it senses that it has become a fishing expedition. In other words, I will not allow a situation to come along in which it will become a fishing expedition, every document is contested as not being authentic. But more or less the -- General Talic's defence has already limited the objection or the contestation to a certain amount of documents. I don't know how many of them. I would imagine that we're talking of hundreds, if not thousands of documents. But I think we have to take it by the ear. Or sometimes it just takes you one witness who was in the know, who has got all the basic information on the authenticity, character of the -- of all those documents, and you could bring forward that person and then one minute bring to nothing all the objections. It depends. You should also be in a position to know to what extent and what qualities and nature the contestation takes shape and from then take it up. I don't think I can help you more than that at this present moment, you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I say, I think, Your Honour, we'll have to see how it develops. But for example, taking Mr. Ackerman's objection that no newspaper article admitted because they're inaccurate. Well, Your Honour, this is not quite the same as in our national jurisdictions. And, Your Honour, we all accept, of course, newspaper articles are inaccurate and that the weight given to them may be different. But that, we would argue, does not per se make them inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, definitely. If Mr. Ackerman is expecting me or the Chamber later on to decide a priori that all newspaper articles are inadmissible because out of their own very nature they are inaccurate or not authentic or whatever, forget it. I mean, with every -- every -- if a newspaper article is on the face of it irrelevant to the case, it will not be admitted. But if, on the face of it, it has some relevance, it will be admitted, and then what probative value it has and what weight it will be given, it's a matter for the Trial Chamber to decide. But I will not exclude an article simply because it's a newspaper article. I have written many articles in my life. So I know what I'm talking about. So I have to wait and see. So that's why I invited you to go through this article, see what it says, and then come back to the Tribunal. I mean, it may be harmless to you. It may be just an opinion by the journalist, or it may contain facts which are damning to your client. I mean, it's for you to read that article and focus on it and tell me where you would -- where you stand, if you want to. Because the question that the Tribunal has is whether to, first, issue a subpoena against the witness or, secondly, to admit his statement -- his written statement together with the article. And then it takes its own course. Of course, there is the problem that arises with regard to cross-examination, because as I have admitted, you have a right to cross-examine the witness. But sometimes dealing with a newspaper article, I doubt how important or how useful or how productive a cross-examination could be, if we're talking of a newspaper article and the journalist who wrote it. So it's up to you to give me feedback on that, and then we'll decide. But up to you definitely. I not going to dismiss an article, a newspaper article, simply because it's a newspaper article. I would be offending all journalists, and it would not reflect what the legal situation should be. I mean, if it's relevant on face value, it should be admitted, and then we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any further matters that you would like to bring up before we bring this Pre-Trial Conference, hopefully the last part, to an end?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- my client is transported back and forth between here and the Detention Centre wearing an extraordinarily heavy bullet-proof vest. I'm given to understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are they trying to protect him against you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not sure. But I'm given to understand that if I make a request from you, they have a much lighter bullet-proof vest that he can wear. And it is -- it is burdensome in the sense that it tends to affect his blood pressure, which is already high. And so there's a medical reason for it. And I understand that if you just instruct security to bring him in the lighter version of the bullet-proof vest, that that will be done. It's also my understanding - and I say this only because I think it might save some time - that General Talic has exactly the same request. And so if you're going to do it, you might as well do it for both of them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you concur with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to consult my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. But if you could consult -- that is, if I make one request, I will make one request for both.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll put forward the same request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't suppose you have any particular objection with regard to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We take a neutral stance on this one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will deal with the problem myself. And I suppose if what you said is correct, there should be no difficulties. Any further --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm just asked to ask Your Honour, in giving Your Honour the witness statements, do you want what we call the attachments, in other words, where witnesses are producing exhibits, documents, personally? Or simply if we give Your Honour the ones we're going to be asking the witness to adduce, or none at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think for the present moment, for the time being, none at all. Then having gone through the witness statement, I might consider that the supporting document or whatever is too important for me not to see beforehand, in which case I will let you -- I will send you a message via the Registrar -- Deputy Registrar to let me have further documentation. But the least, the better.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And thanks for bringing this up. So I think this ought to be returned to Ms. Korner. It belongs to her. So I think we can bring this Pre-Trial Conference to an end. As I told you, you will be receiving a copy of the corrected amended indictment in B/C/S today. I would like you to consider two things, but you will be approached in due course. I mean, one is the possibility of exempting the Court -- the Tribunal from having to read the entire corrected amended indictment in B/C/S to your clients. They have a right to it. But it's up to you to consider that. And secondly, you have the option of either pleading to each count or entering just one plea of "not guilty," I would imagine. I mean, remembering what your clients stated way back in November, the situation hasn't changed since then, except for the decision of the Appeals Chamber. I would be more than happy to have one global plea of "not guilty" and take it from there and move ahead, rather than having to enter a particular plea to each particular count. It is a much more practicable approach, if you are agreeable with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I can do that right now. I can waive the reading, and I can tell you that my client enters a plea of "not guilty" to each and every count as one plea.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do not require the reading out of the indictment, and my client states that he is not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, you just heard what your counsel said. You have just heard what your Defence counsel has said. THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Yes, I have heard it clearly, and I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You agree. General Talic, do you agree with what your counsel has stated? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] I agree absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I expected from both of you. It was not a matter of putting in doubt your Defence counsel. But that solves another issue. We don't have to visit it again on Wednesday. And on Wednesday, we can hopefully start our labours. I thank you. I also thank the interpreters for their -- all their work. And my apologies again for last Friday. I realised yesterday that I kept you 22 minutes beyond what I had promised you I would keep you. But I will make a commendation to the Registrar, letting him know how cooperative you have been throughout. I thank you. I'll see you Wednesday.

procedural_notes.text: [The Judge and Senior Legal Officer confer]
